title: Trees and Graphs
description: Explore hierarchical trees and networked graphs, including terminology, traversals, and common representation strategies.

data.text: Trees and graphs model relationships. Trees organize items hierarchically with a single root and no cycles. Graphs connect items more freely, allowing cycles and multiple paths. Both structures appear throughout computer science, from file systems to social networks.

data.title: Essential tree terms
items: Root: the top node with no parent.
Node: a single element in the tree.
Leaf: a node with no children.
Depth: the number of edges from the root to a node.
Height: the number of edges on the longest path from a node to a leaf.
Binary tree: each node has at most two children.

data.title: Essential graph terms
items: Vertex (node): a single entity in the graph.
Edge: a connection between two vertices.
Directed graph: edges have a direction, like one-way streets.
Undirected graph: edges go both ways.
Weighted graph: edges carry a cost or distance.

data.text: Graphs are usually stored as adjacency lists or adjacency matrices. An adjacency list keeps an array of neighbor lists for each vertex, which is efficient for sparse graphs. An adjacency matrix is a two-dimensional array that records whether an edge exists between every pair of vertices.

Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph layer by layer and is ideal for finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Depth-first search (DFS) dives deep along one branch before backtracking and is useful for cycle detection and topological sorting.

data.title: Breadth-first search
data.content: BFS uses a queue to visit neighbors in order.

data.title: BFS vs DFS
data.text: Use BFS when you need the shortest path or want to explore all options level by level. Use DFS when memory is limited or you need to exhaust one path before moving to the next.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Trees are hierarchical and acyclic; graphs can be cyclic and more general.
Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs; matrices suit dense graphs.
BFS explores by layers; DFS explores by depth.
Choosing the right traversal affects both runtime and memory usage.
data.takeaway: Trees and graphs turn relationships into traversable structures, and knowing how to represent and walk them is essential for advanced algorithm design.
